claims.text: The selected material is a high-entropy alloy containing multiple principal elements.
Thermal processing can systematically modify the alloy's microstructure, including crystal structure, short-range order, and elemental clustering.
The starting alloy is predominantly a single-phase BCC or FCC solid solution.
Processing-induced microstructural changes alter the local atomic environment.
Processing-induced changes in local ordering and compositional fluctuations shift the electronic density of states at the Fermi level.
Changes in the density of states at the Fermi level modify electron–phonon coupling strength.
Electron–phonon coupling governs whether superconducting pairing emerges in the selected alloy.
Electron–phonon coupling governs the superconducting transition temperature of the selected alloy.
A superconducting transition is expected to emerge in specific thermally treated states between 1 and 10 K.
A superconducting high-entropy alloy can have a transition temperature within the proposed 1–10 K test range.
Thermally treated states with microstructural fluctuations that enhance electron–phonon coupling will have a higher superconducting transition temperature than the as-cast baseline.
Such treated states will have a sharper superconducting transition than the as-cast baseline.
The as-cast or minimally processed baseline may show no superconductivity or a lower and broader transition.
The proposed processing effect is expected to apply to near-equiatomic multielement compositions.
The proposed processing effect remains significant only below approximately 10 K.
The proposed processing effect requires processing conditions that preserve a single-phase solid-solution structure.
The effects of configurational entropy on the crystal structure, electronic structure, and superconducting properties of high-entropy alloys remain unclear.
The cited evidence is insufficient to predict exact transition temperatures or their dependence on the proposed microstructural changes.
